opus-5.5.text:
I think the decision came from a fairly simple belief: scaling still works, and we hadn't yet seen the ceiling. A lot of people in the past year started saying the pre-training scaling era is over, that the data is running out, that the gains are flattening. But when we looked at our own experiments, the curves were still going up. Not as dramatically as before, but steadily. And if the curve is still going up, then not pushing further feels like leaving something on the table.

The second reason is about what the base model gives you downstream. Everyone is very excited about reinforcement learning, reasoning, and agents now, and I'm excited about that too. But in my experience, RL mostly *elicits* what's already in the model. It doesn't create knowledge from nothing. If the base model is bigger and has seen more, it has a richer latent space, more world knowledge, better long-tail coverage, and then RL has much more to work with. So in a way, scaling the base is an investment in the ceiling of everything that comes after.

Third, with sparse architectures like MoE, a trillion total parameters doesn't mean a trillion parameters' worth of compute per token. The activated parameters can stay relatively modest. So the question isn't really "can we afford to run a trillion-parameter dense model," it's "can we give the model a much bigger memory while keeping inference cost reasonable." Once you frame it that way, it becomes much more of an engineering problem than a fantasy.

And honestly, part of it is just that you have to try. Many things in this field you can't fully reason out on paper. You only really understand the training stability issues, the infrastructure bottlenecks, the data mixing problems at that scale by actually doing it. If you never go there, you never build that muscle. So for the team, it was also about learning, about being one of the groups that actually knows what happens at that frontier, rather than reading about it in someone else's report.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we didn't start from "we want a trillion parameters." We started from a belief about where the ceiling is, and the trillion came out of that.

When we trained K2, the question we kept asking was: given the compute and data we actually have, what shape of model gets the most intelligence per token? And the data side is the real constraint. High-quality tokens are finite. You can't just keep scaling data the way everyone did in the early scaling-law era, because you run out of good internet. So if data is the bottleneck, the lever you have left is to make each token count more, and the way you do that is more parameters, specifically a sparse MoE where the total parameter count is huge but the activated parameters stay manageable. A trillion total with around 32 billion active is us betting that sparsity is the right way to buy capacity without paying the full inference cost.

The second reason is more about what we wanted the model to do. We were very focused on agentic capabilities, long-horizon tool use, coding, things where the model has to hold a lot of structured knowledge and recall it reliably across many steps. Those abilities seem to depend heavily on total capacity, not just active capacity. A smaller dense model can be fluent, but it forgets, it hallucinates APIs, it loses the thread. We saw in our internal scaling experiments that these behaviors kept improving as we pushed total parameters, and they hadn't plateaued at the scale most open models were at.

And then there's the practical piece, which is that we felt we finally had the training stability to do it. A trillion-parameter run is terrifying because one loss spike can waste weeks of compute. A lot of the work on the optimizer, on MuonClip in particular, was really about making it safe to go that big. Once we were confident we could run that scale without the training blowing up, the question was no longer "can we," it was "why wouldn't we."

So the short version: data is finite, sparsity makes capacity cheap, agentic tasks reward capacity, and we had the stability to attempt it. Those four things together made a trillion feel less like a vanity number and more like the natural next point on the curve.

astra-6.text:
For us, the question wasn’t simply, “Can we build a model with a trillion parameters?” It was, “Can greater capacity give us better performance at a computational cost we can afford?”

That’s why the architecture matters. With a mixture-of-experts model, the total parameter count can be very large, but each token uses only a subset of those parameters. That gives us a way to increase capacity without increasing computation proportionally.

But scale alone isn’t enough. You still need the right data, stable training, and efficient infrastructure. The trillion-parameter number is meaningful only if it translates into better capabilities. That’s the real goal.

sol-6.1.text: For us, the key question was what we could learn by scaling. Could a much larger model deliver meaningful improvements, and could we train it efficiently enough to make those improvements worthwhile? A trillion parameters was a way to explore those questions, rather than an end in itself. The parameter count only matters if it translates into better capabilities.
